# Architecture

## Overview

doc-superpowers is a Claude Code skill that orchestrates documentation generation, auditing, and maintenance through parallel agent dispatch, automated discovery, Mermaid diagram generation, and release note drafting. It supports multiple agent frameworks (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, and Gemini CLI) via plugin manifests (Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI), a symlinked checkout (Codex) and cross-framework tool name mappings. It treats documentation as a first-class engineering artifact with verification gates, evidence-based freshness tracking, opt-in workflow hooks, formal spec lifecycle management, an opt-in work ledger (keyed work items, generated ledger views, related work, in-flight awareness), and cross-cutting README.md/CLAUDE.md synchronization.

## C4 Context Diagram

The system in its operating environment: users invoke the skill through Claude Code, which dispatches agents and interacts with project files and external tools. In a project with `docs/spec-claims/`, the claims verbs also run the host's own adapters; in one with `docs/ledger/config.json`, the work ledger runs its adapters (the GitHub reference adapters reach GitHub through `gh`) and reads and writes refs on the git remote. In one with `docs/search/config.json`, the client also runs doc-search, the opt-in MCP server over the project's docs and code (`references/search.md`); only its optional cloud docs leg leaves the machine, to Vertex AI and Firestore on Google Cloud.

## C4 Container Diagram

Internal components of the skill showing the discovery phase, action router, agent dispatch, template system, hooks engine, merge driver, CI templates, spec claims, the work ledger, doc-search, and spec lifecycle protocol, and the flows between the hooks, `doc-tools.sh` and CI. doc-search is the one component in Python: the uv package `search/`, run by the client as an MCP server through the launcher `install --search` commits, and needed only where `docs/search/config.json` exists. The claims records and the ledger stores live in the target project (and, for the ledger's refs, on its git remote), and the adapters the claims and ledger verbs run are the host's.

## Tech Stack

| Layer | Technology | Purpose |
|-------|-----------|---------|
| Runtime | Claude Code CLI | Hosts the skill, provides Agent/Bash/Read/Write/Grep/Glob tools |
| Skill Format | YAML frontmatter + Markdown | Standard obra/superpowers skill structure |
| Agent Dispatch | Claude Code Agent tool | Parallel Explore and general-purpose agents |
| Diagrams | Mermaid | C4, flowchart, sequence, ERD, state diagram syntax |
| Diagram Rendering | Mermaid MCP (optional) | PNG generation from Mermaid source |
| Discovery | Bash (git, ls), Claude Code Glob tool | Auto-detect project structure and tooling |
| Staleness Detection | `scripts/doc-tools.sh` | 20 subcommands for content hashing (SHA-256) for docs, content identity for code (each code ref's git object id, `code_oids`, recorded by `update-index` — a baseline reset, never a verification, and the only writer of `last_verified` — or, with no baseline reset, as of the doc's own last commit by `build-index`/`add-entry`, and compared with one `git cat-file --batch-check`; record docs such as plans, issues and archived docs are never stale), lossless re-keying when a doc moves (`move-entry`, singly or `--stdin` in a batch — preserves the `code_refs`/`code_oids` pair staleness is derived from, which `remove-entry` + `add-entry` drops, and repoints every other entry's `code_refs`/`code_oids` naming the moved doc), a read-only replay of index merges through the driver (`audit-merges`), in-place `code_refs` edits (`set-code-refs`) and `doc_type` retyping (`set-doc-type`), each singly or `--stdin` in a batch, version management across manifests, ADR/SPEC realization tracking via `implementation-status` / `set-implementation` (the `Implementation:` / `Realized-by:` block surfaced as the `implementation` array in `.doc-index.json`), per-PR release-notes fragments (`fragments list\|validate\|merge`), `tools {install, uninstall, status, version}` for vendoring doc-tools.sh + the CI helpers into a consumer repo (and printing the plugin's version), `claims {validate, run, promote, render, gate, attest, rulings}` for executable spec claims (the Spec Claims row), and `ledger <verb>` for the work ledger (the Work Ledger row; `doc-tools.sh` holds only its dispatch, inert check and verdict helpers). The index is schema v3 (`schema_version` 3, per-ref `code_oids`): every writer stamps 3, a v2 index is read as it is, and an entry without `code_oids` keeps the old commit comparison until it records them (`upgrade-entries` fills them from its `code_commit` with no baseline reset; `update-index` re-baselines it); the field reference is `references/doc-spec.md` → Doc-Index Schema Reference |
| Hooks Installer | Bash (`scripts/hooks/install.sh` + `scripts/hooks/state.sh`) | 3-tier opt-in installer for git hooks (5: `pre-commit`, `post-merge`, `post-checkout`, `prepare-commit-msg`, `pre-push`; plus custom merge driver registration for doc-index.json, alone with `--merge-driver-only`; each check under a budget, `DOC_SUPERPOWERS_HOOK_BUDGET` or `hooks.conf`, default 20 s; with `docs/spec-claims/`, `pre-commit` also runs a blocking claims leg, `claims validate --staged`, and `pre-push` an advisory one, `claims run --planes-of` plus `claims attest --plan`, both with or without a doc-index, and `DOC_SUPERPOWERS_CLAIMS_SKIP=1` bypasses those legs alone), Claude Code hooks (3 scripts: `pre-commit-gate` on PreToolUse, `post-commit-sync` on PostToolUse, `session-summary` on Stop; all three — and the ledger's `ledger-session-notices.sh` — source `hook-lib.sh`, which caps every list and keeps each emitted string under Claude Code's 10,000-character hook-output limit, and runs each check under a watchdog inside the registered 10 s timeout), and CI/CD workflows; plus the work ledger's two opt-in sets, never part of `--all`, refused without `docs/ledger/config.json` and never recorded in `installed.json`: `--ledger` (marked `# ledger-superpowers:begin`/`:end` blocks in pre-commit, pre-push and post-commit) and `--ledger-claude` (SessionStart and PostToolUse `Write|Edit|MultiEdit`, two scripts; `uninstall --claude` keeps `hook-lib.sh` while one of them remains); and doc-search's opt-in `--search` set, under the same rules but refused without `docs/search/config.json`: the launcher `.claude/doc-superpowers/search-mcp.sh` (a byte copy of `scripts/search/launch.sh`) and the `doc-search` entry merged into the project's `.mcp.json`, both committed, reported by `status --json --search` as `.tiers.search`. Acts on `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`; git hooks go to `git rev-parse --git-path hooks` (a `core.hooksPath` from any config but the repository's own is refused). CI tier: the 2 shell workflows by default, the others by name (a retired `doc-index-update.yml` the installer owns is removed on any install) via `--workflows=<csv\|all\|none>` (`--helpers=<bool>` is deprecated and inert: the helpers ship exactly while a workflow runs them, except that `--helpers=false` is refused while `doc-pr-release` is selected or installed); `--force` bypasses state-respect; `--transient` flags an uninstall as non-intentional (will re-install on the next no-flag run); vendoring goes through `doc-tools.sh tools install\|uninstall --helper` (the ledger helper set ships with `doc-ledger-publish` and every claims-running workflow). `state.sh` (sourced by `install.sh`) records the CI tier's workflow set and choices (base branch, cron, strict) in `.claude/doc-superpowers/installed.json` (its own `schema_version` 2, unrelated to the index's) — one read and one write per run, refuses an unreadable file, takes no lock. `install.sh` derives the workflow list from `scripts/hooks/ci/*.yml`. `status` compares every installed hook, local copy, Claude script and settings command with what this install renders (the install date aside), so an install another version made reads outdated; `status --json` is the machine-readable form (`doc-superpowers-hooks-status/1`) |
| CI/CD Templates | GitHub Actions YAML | 9 workflow templates: 3 shell-based (PR freshness check and weekly scheduled audit by default; the opt-in work-ledger views publisher `doc-ledger-publish.yml`, every 30 minutes, which runs `ledger-publish.sh` and, on a ledger host, vendors the ledger helper set; `--workflows=all` skips it on a host without `docs/ledger/config.json`) + 6 Claude-powered AI workflows (feature branch audit+update, PR doc review with @claude interactive, release notes drafting, spec compliance verification, PR full-cycle (review, update, diagram, sync), per-PR release-notes fragment producer `doc-pr-release.yml`). The producer workflow ships with three colocated shell helpers in `doc-pr-release/` (`extract-context.sh`, `update-pr-body.sh`, `commit-and-push.sh`) and a library, `fragment-lib.sh`, that `extract-context.sh`, `commit-and-push.sh` and the step script `verify-fragment.sh` source (`update-pr-body.sh` does not), installed to `.github/scripts/doc-pr-release/`, plus a `RELEASE-NOTES.next/README.md` documenting the fragment-format contract (only dropped if missing — never overwritten). Eleven step scripts in `scripts/hooks/ci/doc-superpowers-steps/` (`claims-check.sh`, `commit-changes.sh`, `freshness-check.sh`, `ledger-publish.sh`, `pr-guard.sh`, `precheck.sh`, `prepare-agent.sh`, `resolve-auth.sh`, `sentinel-check.sh`, `verify-fragment.sh`, `write-context.sh`) hold the step bodies: every `run:` step is a script in `.github/scripts/doc-superpowers-steps/` (the committing steps run a pre-agent snapshot of `commit-changes.sh` from `$RUNNER_TEMP`), with three exceptions: two in `doc-pr-release.yml` — its first step, its pre-checkout PR resolver, which stays inline, and its commit step, `doc-pr-release/commit-and-push.sh` — and `doc-spec-verify.yml`'s amendment step, which runs `doc-pr-release/update-pr-body.sh` and is skipped unless that helper is on disk (`hashFiles`), that is, unless `doc-pr-release` is installed too. The shell templates run the locally-vendored `.github/scripts/doc-tools.sh` (copied by installer) through `freshness-check.sh`, which never reports an unrunnable check as all-current (the PR check warns, or fails under `--ci-strict`; the schedule run and the AI jobs' scope gate fail) and keeps index-sized results in files. All actions are SHA-pinned with exact version comments; every job has `timeout-minutes`. AI workflows pass `github_token: ${{ github.token }}`, install the plugin pinned to the installed version, give the agent a scoped `--allowedTools` and `--max-turns`, run only for same-repository PRs, and never let the agent commit (a checked `commit-changes.sh` step does — for `doc-pr-release`, `commit-changes.sh --check-only` verifies and `commit-and-push.sh` commits; an integrity check, not a sandbox: `references/hooks.md` says what a steered agent can reach). Four of the six (`doc-audit-update`, `doc-review-pr`, `doc-spec-verify`, `doc-pr-full-cycle`) gate on the doc index (`freshness-check.sh scope`) instead of path filters; the producer has its own gate (`paths-ignore` for fragments and RELEASE-NOTES.md, then `write-context.sh`) and the release drafter runs on any push to `release/**` and gates on `precheck.sh`; `doc-spec-verify`'s second job, `claims` (no AI), runs `claims-check.sh pr` on every same-repository, non-Dependabot PR, and the weekly schedule runs `claims-check.sh scheduled` — both report `status=disabled` and run nothing without `docs/spec-claims/`; the three that commit to a branch share one concurrency group per branch, and a run superseded by someone's push ends green where that push re-runs it (`doc-audit-update`, `doc-pr-release`) and fails, asking for a re-run, in `doc-pr-full-cycle`. All 6 AI workflows share a unified auth preflight that prefers `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and falls back to `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (fails fast with a clear error when both are unset; emits `::notice::` when both are set) |
| Docs and Code Search (opt-in) | Python ≥ 3.11 + `uv` (`search/`, `.python-version` 3.12): `semble` 0.7, the MCP Python SDK v2 (`mcp`), `pathspec`; the `cloud` extra adds `google-genai` and `google-cloud-firestore`; the `local-transformer` extra adds `onnxruntime`, `flatbuffers` and `protobuf` (onnxruntime 1.31, or 1.23.2 on Intel macOS). No torch | doc-search, an MCP server (tools `search`, `fetch`, `related`, `status`; CLI `doc-search serve\|init\|index\|query\|status\|eval`) over two semble indexes per worktree — the docs and the code, built from the working tree — fused per file by RRF with an exact-identifier leg, each hit carrying the doc-index's cross-links; an optional cloud docs leg (Vertex AI + Firestore) fused with them, and an opt-in local transformer docs model (`docs.model: "transformer:gte-modernbert-base"`, a per-host vector cache; a static docs index serves while its first build runs). The only Python in the plugin, needed only by a project with `docs/search/config.json`; the launcher `scripts/search/launch.sh` (POSIX sh) runs it through `uv run --frozen --no-dev` (no dev group in a user's environment) |
| doc-search Reference | `references/search.md` | REQUIRED wherever `docs/search/config.json` exists: turning it on, config keys, CLI and exit codes, the tools, the cloud leg's setup and write-path guards, other clients, performance, privacy, troubleshooting; the design is `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-19-doc-search-design.md` |
| Spec Lifecycle Protocol | `references/spec-lifecycle-protocol.md` | Integration guide defining input/output contracts for wrapper skill authors, and the claims Direction protocol (`CODE-DIVERGES`, `DOC-STALE`, `RETIRE`, its policy keys and their defaults) |
| Spec Lifecycle Actions | `references/spec-lifecycle-actions.md` | REQUIRED reference for `spec-generate`, `spec-inject` and `spec-verify`: their detailed procedures and the canonical Spec Status Model |
| Spec Claims | `scripts/doc-tools.sh claims <verb>` + `references/spec-claims.md` | Executable spec claims, opt-in: the directory `docs/spec-claims/` is the switch, and without it every verb prints `{"verb":…,"enabled":false,"exit":0}` (once its command line parses, its dependencies are present and it runs at a repository's top level). `references/spec-claims.md` is REQUIRED while the directory exists. Seven verbs (`validate`, `run`, `promote`, `render`, `gate`, `attest`, `rulings`) with their own exit family: `0`, `1` findings, `2` could not run (never reported as a pass), `3` usage; precedence 1 > 2 > 0. Stores: `config.json` and one sidecar `<DOC-ID>.json` per governing doc in `docs/spec-claims/`; the gate records `gates/<plan-stem>/chunk-<n>.json` and `final.json` (`gate` and `attest --final` write them even when red); the local verdict store `$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/spec-claims/promotions/` (never committed; `promote` writes it); each governing doc's generated `## Claim status` block (`render`, `promote`). Host adapters (a runner per test framework, a log adapter, a config adapter) run from the top level with stdin `/dev/null`, and their output is parsed fail-closed. A range is the branch's own work: its first-parent, non-merge commits plus each first-parent merge's own conflict resolutions (`git show --remerge-diff`, git ≥ 2.36) |
| Work Ledger | `scripts/doc-tools.sh ledger <verb>` + `scripts/ledger/` + `scripts/adapters/` | The work ledger, opt-in: `docs/ledger/config.json` is the switch (`{}` is complete), and without it every verb but `init` prints `ledger: not enabled (no docs/ledger/config.json)` and exits 0. 19 verbs (`show`, `ls`, `find`, `related`, `suggest`, `sweep`, `recheck`, `inflight`, `notices`, `state-watch`, `new`, `assign`, `link`, `note`, `view`, `validate`, `publish`, `finalize`, `init`) sharing the claims exit family (`0`, `1` findings, `2` could not run, `3` usage). `scripts/ledger/lib.sh`, sourced by `doc-tools.sh` when a ledger verb runs in an enabled repository (and for `ledger init` without a config, and for the claims check V5 on a ledger host), sources twelve modules over `*.jq` and `*.awk` programs; bash 3.2 + jq ≥ 1.6, nothing else. Stores: `docs/ledger/` (config, registry, legacy and finalized maps), the item files, the cache `<git common dir>/doc-superpowers/ledger/` (never committed), and on the remote the key counter ref, the in-flight refs and the views branch. Adapters (`pr`, `contracts`, `items`; reference ones for GitHub through `gh`) run fail-closed and are cached by TTL; `DOC_TOOLS_LEDGER_OFFLINE=1` stops adapter runs, fetches and in-flight pushes (key allocation still reaches the counter ref) |
| Work Ledger Reference | `references/ledger.md`, `references/ledger-index.schema.json` | REQUIRED reference for the `ledger` action and wherever `docs/ledger/config.json` exists: config keys and defaults, verbs and exit codes, keys, adapter contracts, in-flight privacy, hooks, `ledger init`; the schema is the index's shape (`ledger-index/1`) |
| Release Procedure | `references/release.md` | REQUIRED reference for `release` (steps 1–12): range start, fragment merge, drafting agent, version bump, release commit, tag |
| Hooks Procedure | `references/hooks.md` | REQUIRED reference for `hooks`: installer routing, the CI consent table (triggers, permissions, what each workflow may commit), and what an AI job's agent can reach |
| Output | Markdown + HTML comments | Generated docs with freshness markers |
| Templates | references/doc-spec.md | Architecture, workflow, spec, ADR, guide, and scope-specific templates |
| Agent Prompt Template | `references/agent-prompt-template.md` | REQUIRED for dispatched review agents: the prompt template (with the trust boundary) and the scope-specific focus areas |
| Output Templates | `references/output-templates.md` | Audit report format (including README.md Status and RELEASE-NOTES.md Status sections, and the Update Tasks that `update --report=<path>` applies) and the spec compliance report format |
| Integration Patterns | `references/integration-patterns.md` | Code review, commit review, and wrapper skill integration patterns |
| Multi-Framework Support | `references/tool-mappings.md` | The one capability matrix: each client's tool for every Claude Code tool the skill names, which hook tiers, subagent and diagram features each client (Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI) supports, and how it resolves `$ROOT` |
| Test Suites | `scripts/test-doc-tools.sh`, `scripts/test-hooks.sh`, `scripts/test-merge-driver.sh`, `scripts/test-doc-pr-release.sh`, `scripts/test-spec-status-model.sh`, `scripts/test-spec-claims.sh`, `scripts/test-ledger.sh`, `scripts/test-helpers.sh` | Seven shell test suites sharing one harness (`test-helpers.sh`) for the bundled freshness tooling, the hooks installer and hooks, the merge driver, the CI templates and their helpers, the skill prompt ↔ tool contract (Spec Status Model, commands the prompts run, evals, packaging), the spec claims checker (`doc-tools.sh claims`) and the work ledger (`doc-tools.sh ledger`, with a 300-item smoke of its budgets; `scripts/bench-ledger.sh 3000` is the full performance check, run by hand, not in CI). Beside them, doc-search's pytest suite (`search/tests/`: never the network — a test-built Model2Vec model, fake Firestore and Vertex). Assertion counts: [CLAUDE.md → Conventions](../../CLAUDE.md#conventions), the one place they are kept. `.github/workflows/tests.yml` runs the shell suites under bash 5.x and `/bin/bash` 3.2, the pytest suite on both legs (after `astral-sh/setup-uv`, pinned by sha), plus `check-version` and a check that this repo's self-installed CI tier matches its templates |
| Evaluation Suite | `evals/evals.json`, `evals/fixtures/` | Skill behavior evaluation tests for measuring accuracy and triggering, plus 15 fixture setups (`evals/fixtures/<eval>/setup.sh`, sharing `lib.sh`) that build each scenario's project; `scripts/test-spec-status-model.sh` runs every one |

## Key Decisions

- **Discovery-first architecture**: Every action runs the discovery phase as its first step, except `hooks` (scaffolding — routes directly to the installer), `release` (parses RELEASE-NOTES.md and commits directly) and `ledger` (routes directly to `doc-tools.sh ledger`). This avoids hardcoding project assumptions and makes the skill work across any project type. Trade-off: slightly slower startup, but significantly more accurate results.

- **Parallel agent dispatch per scope**: Audit and review-pr dispatch one agent per documentation scope in parallel, each with isolated context. This prevents context pollution between unrelated doc reviews and enables concurrent work. Trade-off: more agent invocations, but each is focused and verifiable.

- **In-memory inventory (not persisted)**: The agentic workflow inventory is rebuilt each invocation rather than cached. This ensures freshness at the cost of repeated discovery work. Acceptable because discovery is fast (bash commands) compared to agent review work.

- **Three-layer verification**: Agent evidence → freshness check → human review (SKILL.md Section 2 holds the first two: the dispatched-agent evidence rule and the gate function; the human review of the diff is `update` step 8). No doc update is claimed complete without all three layers passing. This prevents false confidence from partial checks.

- **Template-driven generation**: All doc content follows templates in doc-spec.md rather than freeform generation. This ensures consistency across projects and makes the skill's output predictable and auditable.

- **Graceful degradation**: Missing tools (no Mermaid MCP, no doc-index on first run) trigger fallbacks rather than failures. Freshness tooling is always available (bundled). If doc-index doesn't exist, `check-freshness` exits with `Run build-index first.` — at the skill level, `init` is the action that builds it.

- **Zero skill dependencies**: The skill itself (`skills/doc-superpowers/SKILL.md` + `references/`) has zero dependencies. The bundled tooling in `scripts/` requires bash ≥ 3.2 (macOS's `/bin/bash` included), `git` (≥ 2.25 on a CI runner, where `commit-changes.sh` uses `--pathspec-from-file`; ≥ 2.36 for a claims check over a commit range that holds a merge — `claims run --planes-of`, `claims gate`, and `claims validate`'s V9 over the merge-base range — which reads the merge's hand resolutions with `git show --remerge-diff`; an older git makes that check indeterminate, exit 2), `jq` ≥ 1.6 and `sha256sum`/`shasum`, and otherwise only the POSIX userland stock macOS and Linux ship (no GNU sed, no ripgrep). The work ledger adds nothing required: its GitHub reference adapters need `gh` only when a project's config names them, its key allocation (`cas` mode), in-flight layer and `publish` need a git remote, and `view --open` uses `open` / `xdg-open`. doc-search adds nothing required either: Python and `uv` are needed only by a project that turns it on (`docs/search/config.json`). This makes installation trivial (copy or symlink).

- **Bundled shell tooling**: `scripts/doc-tools.sh` provides freshness tracking as portable shell scripts rather than Python or Node. This ensures zero language dependencies, works on any system with bash/git/jq, and complies with the Agent Skills spec that forbids external runtime requirements for the skill itself. The scripts are bundled (not generated per-project) so they stay versioned with the skill.

- **Content hash + code object ids**: Staleness detection uses SHA-256 content hashes for doc files and, for each code reference, the git object id of its content (a blob, a tree, or a submodule's commit) when the doc was last re-baselined. Commit ids are not used, because squash merges, rebases, cherry-picks and reverts mint new ones for identical bytes. This is deterministic — the tooling reports facts (hash changed, a ref's content changed) and the agent decides what the change means. No heuristic "probably stale" guessing.

- **Audit owns discovery**: Discovery is fundamentally an audit operation — it answers "what exists and what state is it in?" All actions (init, update, diagram, sync) consume the same discovery output rather than duplicating scope detection logic. This single-source-of-truth design prevents drift between what init generates and what audit checks. The audit process also checks RELEASE-NOTES.md currency — counting the commits since the latest entry (after its tag when one exists, else after its date) and reporting any as a P2 finding that points to `release`.

- **README.md/CLAUDE.md sync as cross-cutting concern**: README.md and CLAUDE.md synchronization is not scoped to a single action — it is a cross-cutting concern of every write action: `init` (bootstrap from current codebase state), `update` (propagate structural changes), `sync` (catch accumulated drift), `release` (ensure user-facing docs match the new version) and `spec-generate` (new spec paths). Both files are verified during `audit` for consistency with the skill's actual capabilities and directory structure. In a doc-superpowers CI workflow, `update` and `sync` report the change these files need instead of making it: the checked commit step accepts only `docs/` and the indexed docs.

- **3-tier opt-in hooks**: The hooks system uses three independent tiers (git, Claude Code, CI/CD) that can be installed separately or together. Each tier is opt-in — `hooks install` requires explicit `--git`, `--claude`, `--ci`, or `--all` flags when invoked programmatically. This avoids surprising developers with unwanted automation. The installer is idempotent (safe to re-run) and places everything with git plumbing: it acts on `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` and writes git hooks to `git rev-parse --git-path hooks`, where git runs them (worktrees and submodules included); a `core.hooksPath` from any config but the repository's own (global, system, a command-line `-c`) is refused. It never writes through a symbolic link, and every check runs before the first write. It auto-integrates into an existing shell hook with one marked POSIX block (`# doc-superpowers:begin`/`# doc-superpowers:end`) right after the `#!` line, which runs a locally-copied hook with git's arguments (pre-commit passes the exit code on). Uninstall deletes exactly the marked blocks and the local copies, so the user's files come back byte-for-byte. Claude uninstall removes only the entries running the installer's scripts, and the three scripts and their `hook-lib.sh` — which stays while a work-ledger script that sources it is installed. The work ledger's two sets (`--ledger`, `--ledger-claude`) are opt-in on top of the tiers, never part of `--all`, refused without `docs/ledger/config.json`, and — like the git and Claude tiers — per-clone / per-user and never recorded in `installed.json`; their blocks carry their own markers (`# ledger-superpowers:begin`/`:end`), which never match the tiers'. Status output shows the resolved hooks directory path and distinguishes between owned hooks and integrated hooks. Interactive mode (terminal menu) is reserved for direct CLI invocation only. The git tier also registers a custom merge driver for `docs/.doc-index.json` to auto-resolve index conflicts during merge/rebase.

- **Claude hooks use local copies, per-user**: Claude hook scripts are copied to `.claude/hooks/doc-superpowers/` and registered as `bash "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR"/.claude/hooks/doc-superpowers/<hook>.sh`, so they run whatever the cwd. They find `doc-tools.sh` by the merge driver's rule (newest version-named plugin-cache sibling, or a checkout's own path), so a plugin update needs no re-install. The copies and `.claude/settings.local.json` hold this machine's paths, so the tier is per-user: both are excluded from git through `info/exclude`, and each contributor installs their own.

- **Claude hook settings use nested matcher format**: Hook entries in `.claude/settings.local.json` use the nested `{ matcher, hooks: [{ type, command, timeout }] }` structure required by Claude Code. Events are keyed under `.hooks.PreToolUse`, `.hooks.PostToolUse`, and `.hooks.Stop`; `--ledger-claude` adds `.hooks.SessionStart` and a second `PostToolUse` group (matcher `Write|Edit|MultiEdit`). The installer merges per entry: an entry is its own only when its command runs one of its scripts (three for `--claude`, two for `--ledger-claude`), so every other entry and group survives install and uninstall byte-for-byte. Note: hook source templates contain the `__DOC_TOOLS_RESOLVE__` placeholder that is only resolved by the installer at install time — manual hook entries in settings files will contain unresolved placeholders and will not function correctly. The installer is the sole authority for hook registration.

- **Hooks report, never re-baseline**: No hook runs `update-index` or writes `docs/.doc-index.json`: re-baselining a doc is a reviewer's act. The git `pre-commit` hook judges the staged tree (`check-freshness --tree "$(git write-tree)"`, which reads the index and the docs from that tree as well as the code refs), so it sees exactly the commit being made — scoped to the staged paths plus every entry the staged index adds; an indexed doc the commit leaves out is "not in this commit" (`git add` it) when it is on disk, "missing from disk" only when it is gone. The Claude hooks follow the harness contract: the event arrives as JSON on stdin, and the reply goes out as JSON (`additionalContext` for Claude, `systemMessage` for the user), or as exit 2 with a stderr reason under STRICT. The gate defers commands that stage as they commit to the git hook, which sees the real index. `Stop` fires after every response, so the summary is scoped to working-tree changes and bounded (2 s, process-group watchdog). In the `--git` and `--claude` tiers, absent tooling is silent and a failing freshness check prints one line and blocks only under STRICT. The work ledger's git legs judge differently (*Work ledger* below): their pre-commit blocks on any non-zero exit, their pre-push refuses, and their post-commit pushes to the remote; none of them writes the index either. The git tier's claims legs, which run whenever `docs/spec-claims/` exists, index or not, judge differently: in pre-commit a claims finding blocks the commit whatever STRICT says, and a claims check that cannot run blocks only under STRICT; pre-push's leg only reports (*Spec claims: opt-in, inert, never a false pass*). Trade-off: the Claude gate decides only pre-staged commits; the rest rely on the git tier.

- **Spec claims: opt-in, inert, never a false pass**: Executable spec claims (`doc-tools.sh claims <verb>`, `references/spec-claims.md`) are switched on by the directory `docs/spec-claims/` and by nothing else. Without it every verb prints `{"verb":…,"enabled":false,"exit":0}` and exits 0 — once its command line parses, its dependencies are present and it runs at a repository's top level, which every run needs — and the git hooks, the CI templates and the spec actions behave as they did before claims existed. The verbs keep their own exit family (`0`; `1` findings; `2` could not run; `3` usage; precedence 1 > 2 > 0) instead of the index verbs' table, so "could not run" — an adapter reporting `indeterminate` or missing, a base that does not resolve, a dirty tree where one is refused — is exit 2 and is never reported as a pass. Every consumer keeps that split: the pre-commit leg blocks on a finding whatever STRICT says and on a check that could not run only under STRICT; the pre-push leg reports; `doc-spec-verify`'s `claims` job fails on findings, and on a check that could not run only under `--ci-strict`; the weekly schedule keeps its issue open on findings and fails when nothing could run. The checks themselves are the host's: claims bind to the host's tests, logs and configuration through small executables it names in `config.json`, so doc-superpowers stays language-agnostic. With the work ledger on, V5 judges a tracker that names a ledger item by the ledger's status classes (so `Won't Fix` closes it), reading the index offline; a ledger that cannot be read is one indeterminate V5 row, never a pass. Gate records are self-reported: `attest` proves they are consistent with the tree (patch ids, reconciliations, rulings and promotions, verdicts re-run at HEAD), not that an agent ran them, and a ruling's `by` principal is recorded, never verified. Trade-off: a second verdict path beside freshness, which the opt-in keeps out of every project that has not asked for it; `update-index` stays a baseline reset, and a verification verdict comes only from claims.

- **Work ledger: the issue is the source of truth; everything else is derived**: An opt-in verb group (`doc-tools.sh ledger`, `references/ledger.md`; design `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-12-work-ledger-design.md`) switched on by `docs/ledger/config.json` and inert without it — every verb but `init` prints one `not enabled` line and exits 0, and the hooks, CI templates and spec actions behave as before. The decisions that shape it: an item is an issue file (or a hosted issue through an adapter) and every row, page and status the ledger shows is computed from it, so nothing can disagree with an item; views are generated and never edited, and `publish` writes them to an orphan branch with git plumbing, never touching HEAD, the index or the working tree; keys are allocated by compare-and-swap on a counter ref on the remote, so two branches or machines never take one number, with provisional keys offline that `finalize` replaces (or, in `merge` mode for fork-and-PR repositories, that a maintainer finalizes on the base); relations are data, named contracts an item `changes` or `consumes`, never prose; work in flight is visible across machines through in-flight refs the post-commit leg pushes, and notices are pulled at pause points (the SessionStart hook, the per-chunk `notices --gate` task `spec-inject` injects), never pushed into a session; and everything project-specific is an adapter, run fail-closed (exit 2, never a silent clean) and cached by TTL, so no verb touches the network unless asked or a cache has expired. The ledger reads `docs/.doc-index.json` and never writes it. Its git legs are the one place a doc-superpowers hook blocks without STRICT: pre-commit on any non-zero `validate --staged` (a check that could not run included), pre-push on a provisional key the branch adds (since its merge-base with config `base`) in `cas` mode; and its post-commit leg is the one hook that writes to the remote — in the background, never prompting, logging to `push.log`. Trade-off: enabling the in-flight layer publishes local branch names (under a host pseudonym unless the user names one) to the shared remote.

- **doc-search: one server, two semble indexes, opt-in, outside the core**: The docs-and-code search server (`search/`, `references/search.md`; design `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-19-doc-search-design.md`) is switched on by `docs/search/config.json` and answers the inert line without it. It keeps two semble indexes per worktree — docs and code — rather than one: BM25 statistics stay per corpus, semble's code reranking applies to code only, and the eval measured one shared index 0.04 recall@10 / 0.07 MRR below the pair. It joins them in the server (one call, one ranking, the doc-index's `code_refs` as cross-links) instead of in the agent. Local by default, with static Model2Vec models and no transformer runtime. The docs index can opt in to a local transformer (`docs.model: "transformer:gte-modernbert-base"`; design `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-20-doc-search-local-transformer-design.md`): it gains on paraphrase queries and costs a first build of hours per host, so that build runs in a lane of its own, under a host-wide encoder lock, into a per-host content-addressed encode cache, while a static docs index answers; it needs the `local-transformer` extra, which the launcher adds. The optional cloud leg (Vertex + Firestore) is fused, never a replacement, and its shared corpus is written only from the base branch, through a stamp decision table, a repository identity check, a lease and a prune cap. It is the plugin's one Python component, so it lives outside the bash + jq core: nothing in `scripts/doc-tools.sh` or the hooks depends on it.

- **Spec lifecycle as composable primitives**: The three spec lifecycle actions (`spec-generate`, `spec-inject`, `spec-verify`) are context-agnostic — they have zero knowledge of which wrapper skill invokes them. This keeps doc-superpowers decoupled from any specific development workflow. Wrapper skills wire the actions into their pipelines at 5 interception points (post-brainstorm, during-plan, during-execute, pre-finish, during-review) using the contracts defined in `references/spec-lifecycle-protocol.md`.

- **Spec lifecycle protocol as a reference doc**: The integration guide for wrapper authors lives in `references/spec-lifecycle-protocol.md` rather than inline in SKILL.md. This separates the "how to use these actions" (protocol doc, aimed at wrapper authors) from "what these actions do" (SKILL.md, aimed at the skill runtime). Wrapper authors read the protocol doc; the skill engine reads SKILL.md.

- **Agent-assisted release note drafting**: The `release` action uses agent-assisted drafting with conventional commit parsing to generate RELEASE-NOTES.md entries. Before drafting it runs `doc-tools.sh fragments merge <previous release | ROOT> HEAD` (the previous release: its tag, else the commit that added its RELEASE-NOTES.md heading) over the `RELEASE-NOTES.next/PR-*.md` fragments produced by the `doc-pr-release.yml` CI workflow. Consumption is recorded only by deleting a fragment in the release commit, so a fragment is unreleased while it is present — also one merged after an earlier release branch was cut. Each fragment is merged losslessly (units deduped, sections folded onto one vocabulary) or skipped with a warning and kept for the next release; drifted hashes (human edits) are merged as written, with a warning. The release commit deletes exactly the consumed fragments (`--remove`), and it must reach `main`: until it does, `fragments merge` refuses rather than release those fragments twice. During release, CLAUDE.md and README.md are synchronized to reflect the current state of the skill, and `bump-version` + `check-version` enforce manifest version consistency before tagging. The action offers backfill tagging for releases that were cut without a git tag.

- **Formal spec tracking with drift detection**: `spec-inject` (execute phase) distinguishes between alignment (implementation achieves spec intent) and drift (implementation contradicts spec). Aligned changes update spec status and Implementation Notes only when the **Spec Status Model** permits — the spec must be an implementation *target* rather than a constraint reference or an amendment, it must sit at a ladder status, the transition must move forward, and — in a claims-enabled project (`docs/spec-claims/` exists) — its claims must clear the final gate (**Spec Status Model → R5**). Drifted changes are flagged for human review without auto-modifying spec content; in a claims-enabled project the direction (`CODE-DIVERGES`, `DOC-STALE` or `RETIRE`) is ruled and recorded on the claim before either side is edited (`references/spec-lifecycle-protocol.md`, Direction protocol). This prevents the system from silently papering over design divergences while still reducing manual bookkeeping for routine updates. This page summarizes; it does not define — the canonical rules live in the **Spec Status Model** section of `references/spec-lifecycle-actions.md`.

- **Custom merge driver for doc-index**: The git tier registers a merge driver (`scripts/merge-doc-index.sh`) for `docs/.doc-index.json`. Git runs it for merge, rebase, cherry-pick and revert. It is a base-aware, per-key three-way merge in jq: an entry that only one side changed or deleted takes that side. An entry both sides changed is merged field by field. The side that changed a field wins, and a field both sides changed goes to the entry with the newer `last_verified` (non-null beats null). The verification record (`content_hash`, `code_oids`, `code_commit`, `last_verified`) moves as one unit, so a merge never records a baseline for a doc/code pair nobody re-baselined, and `deprecated` wins. The driver does not guess in three per-entry cases, and each leaves `git merge-file` conflict markers, exits 1 and names the doc key on stderr (the first also names the fields). The first is a field both sides changed where `last_verified` does not order them. That is the usual case for two edits of one field, because only `update-index` writes `last_verified`: two `set-code-refs` runs, a repoint against a re-deprecation, or two same-second re-baselines with different results all tie. Two ties are merged rather than refused: `code_refs` both sides rewrote as in-place substitutions (two branches that each moved a different doc the entry cites, or a repoint beside an added ref) take one side's substitutions applied to the other's list, when the result holds exactly the refs a three-way set merge keeps (tried also when `last_verified` orders the sides, before the newer side's list wins whole); and a verification record whose `last_verified` is still the base's on both sides (neither re-baselined the entry), with `content_hash` and `code_commit` agreeing, merges `code_oids` key by key. The second is an entry deleted on one side and changed on the other, unless the deleting side re-keyed it (`move-entry`: a new key whose entry is the old one but for `content_hash`, the only such key, absent from the other side): then the other side's change is merged into the new key by the same field rules and the old key dropped (GH #33; the match and its ambiguity cases are in `references/doc-spec.md` → *Re-keys in a merge*). The third is an entry that is not an object on every side. A failure of the whole file gets the same treatment but names no key: an input (ours, theirs or the base) that is not a single index object, `jq` missing, a scratch file that cannot be created, or a signal mid-write. The top level and key order start from ours, with no regenerated `generated_at`/`build_commit` and no re-sort. For a given pair of commits, the result is deterministic. The registered command resolves the driver at merge time: the newest version-named plugin-cache sibling, or a checkout's own copy. The path is quoted, and no driver found gives conflict markers. The driver keeps routine index updates on two branches from conflicting locally. GitHub's mergeability check does not run custom drivers.

- **Granular CI install with state-respect**: The CI tier supports per-workflow install/uninstall via `--workflows=<csv|all|none>`, with persistent install-state in `.claude/doc-superpowers/installed.json` (managed by `scripts/hooks/state.sh`). A workflow that was uninstalled intentionally is NOT re-added on the next no-flag `install --ci` — preserving user intent across re-runs. `--force` bypasses state-respect; `--transient` flags an uninstall as non-intentional so the next install re-adds it. Explicit `--workflows=<name>` always beats state-respect on the rationale that "explicit > implicit." (`all` also leaves out `doc-ledger-publish` on a host without the ledger, with a note: its 30-minute cron would bill no-op runs.) The state file is committed to the repo so install choices persist across contributors: it records the workflow set and the choices (base branch, cron, strict), so a plain re-install — the upgrade path — reproduces them instead of resetting them. A workflow on disk counts as installed whatever the state says; with no state file, the workflows on disk are the set and a pre-3.0 install's choices are read back from them. An unreadable state file (a merge conflict) is refused, never overwritten. The default set is the 2 shell workflows; the others — the Claude-powered ones and the shell `doc-ledger-publish` — are opt-in by name. The installer takes no lock, so runners that parallelize installs into one repository should wrap them in one. `install.sh` derives the canonical workflow list from `scripts/hooks/ci/*.yml` (`state.sh` only records it), so dropping a new template into the directory is automatically picked up.
